```{r}
#| label: setup
needed <- c("rsample", "rpart", "rpart.plot", "ranger", "xgboost", "yardstick")
missing <- needed[!vapply(needed, requireNamespace, logical(1), quietly = TRUE)]
if (length(missing)) stop("Install these packages in the Console: ",
                          paste(missing, collapse = ", "))
if (packageVersion("xgboost") < "3.0.0") stop("Update xgboost to version 3 or later.")
library(rsample)
library(rpart)
library(rpart.plot)
library(ranger)
library(xgboost)
library(yardstick)
options(scipen = 999, width = 80)

# Number of splits in a tree.
n_splits <- function(tree) sum(tree$frame$var != "<leaf>")
# Area under the ROC curve, with Yes (a bump) as the event.
auc <- function(y, p) roc_auc_vec(y, p, event_level = "second")
# The four counts at the 0.50 threshold. TP: bumps named bumps.
# FP: other faults named bumps. FN: bumps missed. TN: other faults left as No.
four <- function(y, p) {
  yes <- y == "Yes"
  c(TP = sum(p >= .5 & yes), FP = sum(p >= .5 & !yes),
    FN = sum(p < .5 & yes), TN = sum(p < .5 & !yes))
}
score <- function(y, p) c(AUC = auc(y, p),
  accuracy = mean((p >= .5) == (y == "Yes")), four(y, p))
```

# Keep comparison and test faults separate

Training faults are 70% of the dataset and test faults are the other 30%. Inside training, 80% are analysis faults and 20% are validation faults. Both splits keep the share of bumps about the same in each part. Every model is grown and tuned on the analysis faults and compared on the validation faults. Only the model you choose is estimated again on all training faults, and it predicts the test faults once. The random split draws faults, not settings, so the same setting can appear in training and in test.

```{r}
#| label: split
set.seed(467)
outer <- initial_split(d, prop = .70, strata = y)
train <- training(outer)
test <- testing(outer)
set.seed(467)
inner <- initial_split(train, prop = .80, strata = y)
analysis <- training(inner)
validation <- testing(inner)
# Each fault is in exactly one part. These sizes are the same on every computer.
stopifnot(nrow(train) == 1358, nrow(test) == 583,
          nrow(analysis) == 1085, nrow(validation) == 273,
          !any(test$row_id %in% train$row_id),
          !any(validation$row_id %in% analysis$row_id),
          setequal(c(train$row_id, test$row_id), d$row_id),
          setequal(c(analysis$row_id, validation$row_id), train$row_id))
sapply(list(analysis = analysis, validation = validation, test = test), nrow)
# Bumps in analysis and validation, the share of No in analysis, and test faults whose setting is also in training.
sapply(list(analysis = analysis, validation = validation),
       function(z) sum(z$y == "Yes"))
mean(analysis$y == "No")
sum(test$setting %in% train$setting)
```

# Grow and prune a classification tree

A node's Gini impurity is the probability that two faults drawn at random from the node, with replacement, carry different labels. With $p$ the node's share of bumps,

$$G = 2p(1-p).$$

$G$ is 0 when the node holds only one label and largest, 0.5, when half are bumps. A split sends $n_L$ faults to the left child and $n_R$ to the right. Its weighted Gini impurity, and the drop from the parent node, are

$$G_{\text{split}} = \frac{n_L G_L + n_R G_R}{n_L + n_R}, \qquad \text{drop} = G_{\text{parent}} - G_{\text{split}}.$$

The tree takes the split with the largest drop.

Cost-complexity pruning trades classification error against the number of leaves. The complexity parameter (CP) is the penalty for one more leaf in `rpart`, as a share of the root node's error. The code grows a large tree first, with `cp = 0`, and then prunes it back.

Ten-fold cross-validation (CV) inside the analysis faults gives `xerror` and `xstd` for each subtree. `xerror` is the CV classification error divided by the error of the tree with no split. It is not AUC. `xstd` is its standard error. The one-standard-error (one-SE) rule takes the smallest subtree whose `xerror` is no more than the minimum `xerror` plus that minimum's `xstd`. The code below finds both subtrees from the table.

```{r}
#| label: trees
tree_controls <- rpart.control(cp = 0, maxdepth = 30, minsplit = 20, minbucket = 7,
                               xval = 10)
set.seed(467)
full <- rpart(y ~ ., data = analysis[, c("y", predictors)], method = "class",
  parms = list(split = "gini"), control = tree_controls)
ct <- full$cptable
low <- which.min(ct[, "xerror"])
pick <- min(which(ct[, "xerror"] <= ct[low, "xerror"] + ct[low, "xstd"]))
# A CP just above the table value keeps exactly the subtree on that line.
tree_min <- prune(full, cp = ct[low, "CP"] * (1 + 1e-9))
tree_1se <- prune(full, cp = ct[pick, "CP"] * (1 + 1e-9))
root_error <- min(mean(analysis$y == "Yes"), mean(analysis$y == "No"))
round(ct, 5)
tree_summary <- data.frame(rule = c("minimum CV", "one SE"),
  splits = c(n_splits(tree_min), n_splits(tree_1se)), CP = ct[c(low, pick), "CP"],
  CV_error = ct[c(low, pick), "xerror"] * root_error)
tree_summary
leaves <- ct[, "nsplit"] + 1
plot(leaves, ct[, "xerror"], type = "b", log = "x", pch = 19,
  ylim = range(ct[, "xerror"] - ct[, "xstd"], ct[, "xerror"] + ct[, "xstd"]),
  xlab = "Leaves (log scale)", ylab = "CV error relative to the root")
arrows(leaves, ct[, "xerror"] - ct[, "xstd"], leaves, ct[, "xerror"] + ct[, "xstd"],
  angle = 90, code = 3, length = .03, col = "grey50")
abline(h = ct[low, "xerror"] + ct[low, "xstd"], lty = 2, col = "#C41230")
```

# Bagging, a random forest and out-of-bag predictions

Bagging grows many trees, each on a bootstrap sample of the analysis faults, and averages their probabilities. A random forest does the same, but each split may try only some of the predictors, drawn at random. `mtry` is the number of predictors a split may try. Bagging uses all $p$ predictors. The default forest uses $\lfloor\sqrt p\rfloor$. Neither can be read as rules the way the pruned tree can.

Each bootstrap sample leaves out some faults. The out-of-bag (OOB) prediction for a fault averages only the trees that did not see it, so those averages estimate how the forest would score a new fault. With $\hat p_i$ the OOB probability of a bump for fault $i$, $y_i = 1$ for a bump and 0 otherwise, and $n$ analysis faults,

$$\text{OOB error} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} \mathbf{1}\big[(\hat p_i \ge 0.50) \ne (y_i = 1)\big], \qquad \text{Brier score} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} (\hat p_i - y_i)^2.$$

The OOB error counts wrong labels at the 0.50 threshold. The Brier score is the mean squared gap between the probability and the label, so a bump given 0.10 adds 0.81 and a bump given 0.45 adds 0.30. For a probability forest, ranger reports the Brier score as `prediction.error`. The code computes the OOB error itself.

```{r}
#| label: ensembles
# num.threads = 1 and seed = 467 make a second run on your own computer
# match the first. A neighbour on another operating system can differ in
# the third decimal. Compare your bagging with your forest, not with a neighbour.
p <- length(predictors)
forest_mtry <- floor(sqrt(p))
bag <- ranger(y ~ ., data = analysis[, c("y", predictors)], num.trees = 500,
  mtry = p, probability = TRUE, seed = 467, num.threads = 1)
forest <- ranger(y ~ ., data = analysis[, c("y", predictors)], num.trees = 500,
  mtry = forest_mtry, probability = TRUE, importance = "permutation",
  seed = 467, num.threads = 1)
oob <- data.frame(model = c("bagging", "forest"), mtry = c(p, forest_mtry),
  error = c(mean((bag$predictions[, "Yes"] >= .5) != (analysis$y == "Yes")),
            mean((forest$predictions[, "Yes"] >= .5) != (analysis$y == "Yes"))),
  Brier = c(bag$prediction.error, forest$prediction.error))
oob
```

# Which measurements does the forest rely on?

Permutation importance shuffles one predictor across the OOB faults and records how much the OOB Brier score rises. A large rise means the forest's predictions depend on that predictor. Read each bar against what that predictor measures. Some predictors share almost the same information.

```{r}
#| label: importance
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 5
importance <- sort(forest$variable.importance, decreasing = TRUE)
round(importance, 5)
par(mar = c(4, 12, 2, 1))
barplot(rev(head(importance, 10)), horiz = TRUE, las = 1, cex.names = .8,
  col = "#156082", border = NA, xlab = "Increase in OOB Brier score")
par(mar = c(5.1, 4.1, 4.1, 2.1))
print(cor(analysis$Y_Minimum, analysis$Y_Maximum), digits = 12)
```

# Boosting and its learning rate

Boosting adds small trees one after another. Each new tree is fit to the residuals left by the trees before it. The learning rate scales how much each new tree adds, and the depth limits the splits along any path. Keep depth 3 and compare rates 0.05 and 0.5 on the same five CV folds inside the analysis faults.

Log-loss grades the probabilities. For one fault it is $-\log \hat p_i$ if the fault is a bump and $-\log(1-\hat p_i)$ if it is not, so a wrong probability near 0 or 1 adds much more than one near one half. Lower is better. `test_logloss_mean` is the mean loss on the held-out CV folds, not on the test faults. `train_logloss_mean` is the loss on the folds used to grow the trees.

```{r}
#| label: boost-cv
dm <- xgb.DMatrix(analysis[, predictors], label = as.numeric(analysis$y == "Yes"))
set.seed(467)
cv_slow <- xgb.cv(params = list(objective = "binary:logistic", eval_metric = "logloss",
  learning_rate = .05, max_depth = 3, nthread = 1), data = dm,
  nrounds = 1000, nfold = 5, verbose = 0)
set.seed(467)
cv_fast <- xgb.cv(params = list(objective = "binary:logistic", eval_metric = "logloss",
  learning_rate = .5, max_depth = 3, nthread = 1), data = dm,
  nrounds = 1000, nfold = 5, verbose = 0)
slow <- cv_slow$evaluation_log
fast <- cv_fast$evaluation_log
boost_table <- data.frame(rate = c(.05, .5),
  rounds = c(which.min(slow$test_logloss_mean), which.min(fast$test_logloss_mean)),
  min_logloss = c(min(slow$test_logloss_mean), min(fast$test_logloss_mean)),
  loss_1000 = c(slow$test_logloss_mean[1000], fast$test_logloss_mean[1000]),
  train_1000 = c(slow$train_logloss_mean[1000], fast$train_logloss_mean[1000]))
boost_table
plot(slow$iter, slow$test_logloss_mean, type = "l", col = "#156082",
  ylim = range(slow$test_logloss_mean, fast$test_logloss_mean),
  xlab = "Rounds", ylab = "Log-loss on held-out folds")
lines(fast$iter, fast$test_logloss_mean, col = "#C41230")
legend("topright", c("rate 0.05", "rate 0.5"), col = c("#156082", "#C41230"),
  lty = 1, bty = "n")
# The rate with the lower CV minimum, and the number of rounds at that minimum.
k <- which.min(boost_table$min_logloss)
boost_rate <- boost_table$rate[k]
boost_rounds <- boost_table$rounds[k]
set.seed(467)
boost <- xgboost(x = analysis[, predictors], y = analysis$y, nrounds = boost_rounds,
  learning_rate = boost_rate, max_depth = 3, nthreads = 1)
```

# Compare the candidates on the same validation faults

The area under the ROC curve (AUC), where ROC is the receiver operating characteristic, measures ranking. It is the probability that a randomly drawn bump gets a higher predicted probability than a randomly drawn other fault, with a tie counting as half. 0.5 is no better than random ordering and 1 is a perfect ordering. Yes is the second level of `y`, so `event_level = "second"`. Accuracy and the four counts use the fixed 0.50 threshold. The dataset gives no cost for a missed bump or a false one, so the threshold stays at 0.50.

```{r}
#| label: validation
p_validation <- list(
  tree_min = predict(tree_min, validation, type = "prob")[, "Yes"],
  tree_1se = predict(tree_1se, validation, type = "prob")[, "Yes"],
  bagging = predict(bag, validation, num.threads = 1)$predictions[, "Yes"],
  forest = predict(forest, validation, num.threads = 1)$predictions[, "Yes"],
  boosting = predict(boost, validation[, predictors]))
validation_results <- data.frame(model = names(p_validation),
  t(sapply(p_validation, function(pr) score(validation$y, pr))), row.names = NULL)
stopifnot(all(rowSums(validation_results[c("TP", "FP", "FN", "TN")]) ==
              nrow(validation)))
validation_results
c(always_No_accuracy = mean(validation$y == "No"))
dotchart(setNames(validation_results$AUC, validation_results$model),
  xlim = c(.5, 1), xlab = "Validation AUC", pch = 19, col = "#156082")
```

# Check unseen settings inside training

Run this after you have recorded your choice, and do not change the choice because of it. In the random split, most test faults share a setting with some training fault. The last number printed by the split chunk counts them. This check scores the models on validation faults whose setting no analysis fault has.

The split below stays inside the training faults and keeps whole settings together, so no setting appears on both sides. It is the grouped split from the trees slides, `group_initial_split`, with the plate setting from the prepare chunk as the group.

For comparison, the code grows and prunes a new one-SE tree on the grouped analysis faults. Your chosen model keeps its locked settings, so boosting keeps the rate and rounds from Question 8.

```{r}
#| label: grouped-check
set.seed(467)
grouped <- group_initial_split(train, group = setting, prop = .80)
ga <- training(grouped)
gv <- testing(grouped)
stopifnot(length(intersect(unique(ga$setting), unique(gv$setting))) == 0,
  nrow(ga) + nrow(gv) == nrow(train), !any(c(ga$row_id, gv$row_id) %in% test$row_id))
group_counts <- c(analysis = nrow(ga), validation = nrow(gv),
  analysis_Yes = sum(ga$y == "Yes"), validation_Yes = sum(gv$y == "Yes"),
  shared_settings = length(intersect(unique(ga$setting), unique(gv$setting))))
group_counts
set.seed(467)
gfull <- rpart(y ~ ., data = ga[, c("y", predictors)], method = "class",
  control = tree_controls)
gct <- gfull$cptable
glow <- which.min(gct[, "xerror"])
gpick <- min(which(gct[, "xerror"] <= gct[glow, "xerror"] + gct[glow, "xstd"]))
gtree <- prune(gfull, cp = gct[gpick, "CP"] * (1 + 1e-9))
p_group_tree <- predict(gtree, gv, type = "prob")[, "Yes"]
if (my_model %in% c("tree_min", "tree_1se")) {
  gi <- if (my_model == "tree_min") glow else gpick
  gm <- prune(gfull, cp = gct[gi, "CP"] * (1 + 1e-9))
  p_group <- predict(gm, gv, type = "prob")[, "Yes"]
} else if (my_model %in% c("bagging", "forest")) {
  gm <- ranger(y ~ ., data = ga[, c("y", predictors)], num.trees = 500,
    mtry = locked$mtry, probability = TRUE, seed = 467, num.threads = 1)
  p_group <- predict(gm, gv, num.threads = 1)$predictions[, "Yes"]
} else {
  set.seed(467)
  gm <- xgboost(x = ga[, predictors], y = ga$y, nrounds = locked$rounds,
    learning_rate = locked$rate, max_depth = 3, nthreads = 1)
  p_group <- predict(gm, gv[, predictors])
}
group_results <- rbind(one_SE_tree = score(gv$y, p_group_tree),
  chosen_model = score(gv$y, p_group))
stopifnot(all(rowSums(group_results[, c("TP", "FP", "FN", "TN")]) == nrow(gv)))
group_results
c(tree_random_AUC = auc(validation$y, p_validation$tree_1se),
  chosen_random_AUC = auc(validation$y, p_validation[[my_model]]))
```
